title: G96 CSS requires G50 max-RPM cap
body: G96 (constant surface speed) turning MUST carry a G50 S<max-rpm> cap or controller equivalent — without it a small-diameter finish pass over-spins the chuck and ejects the part. Missing G50 on a G96 program is a -20 quality penalty and a crash risk.

title: Boring-bar L/D limit
body: Boring-bar deflection scales L^4/D^4 (worse than a mill end-mill's L^3). Keep L/D <= 4 for steel bars, <= 6 for carbide-shanked, else expect ID chatter, taper, and scrapped bores. The bar is the dominant lever, not feed/speed.

title: Single-point threading entry-lock + multi-pass
body: Single-point threading needs a position-locked entry (G76 or G92 canned cycle) plus a multi-pass infeed schedule — a feed-mode entry cuts a non-helical first revolution and single-pass overloads the final flank. Prefer modern G76 over legacy G92 single-block.

title: Sub-spindle handoff 0.5-degree phase tolerance
body: On a mill-turn, sub-spindle pickup must align cutoff timing within 0.5 degrees of spindle phase; outside that window the transfer collides or drops the part. Verify via SubSpindleHandoffVerifierEngine before emitting a transfer block.

title: JM Die lathe fleet is 100% Okuma OSP
body: JM Die's entire lathe fleet (LTH-01..07) is 100% Okuma OSP. Default lathe work to Okuma OSP dialect (G-code variants, G95 feed/rev, special-G, macro syntax) — assuming Fanuc defaults misprograms every JM Die job. IPR vs IPM confusion is a 10x feed error (-25).

title: Parting/grooving deep-slot peck
body: Parting/grooving deeper than 3x the tool width traps chips against the narrow blade and snaps it (often into the chuck). Use a peck-grooving cycle (G75 Q-parameter) above depth ratio 3, and gate blade L/t on chatter + stress-to-yield before lights-out.

title: Avoiding Crashes in CNC Machines

title: Load Sensing Systems in CNC Machines

title: Backlash in CNC Machines
body: High backlash can lead to cutter chatter and workpiece gouging, especially with dull cutting tools. It affects precision operations involving axis movement reversals.

title: Compensating for Backlash in CNC Machines
body: Backlash can be compensated for if the amount is precisely known using linear encoders or manual measurement, by zeroing the mechanism against a reference object.

title: Shim in Shell Mills

title: Conventional vs Climb Milling

title: Adjusting Tool Radius for Tolerance

title: Diameter Selection for Milling Cutters

title: Flute Count and Feed Rate Balance
body: More flutes allow higher feed rates but reduce room for swarf, so a balance must be chosen.

title: Coating Benefits for Milling Cutters

title: Helix Angle Considerations

title: Importance of Tool Angles

title: Nose Radius Effect
body: A nose radius on the cutting point creates radii when cutting corners in the workpiece and extends the life of the tool tip, but it also increases machining forces.

title: Tool Holder Rigidity
body: The tool bit is held with a rigid tool holder during operation to ensure stability and prevent chatter.

title: Turning Forces
body: Three principal forces in turning are the cutting force, axial force, and radial force. These must be accounted for to avoid workpiece breakage, deformation, and chatter.

title: Speeds and Feeds Considerations
body: Speeds and feeds are chosen based on workpiece material, cutter material, setup rigidity, machine tool rigidity, spindle power, and coolant usage.

title: Chatter on Machined Surfaces
body: Poor surface finish, known as chatter, is evident by an undulating or regular finish of waves on the machined surfaces of a workpiece. This can be caused by incorrect clamping, a dull tool, or inappropriate presentation of a device.

title: Cutting Conditions in Machining
body: Speed, feed, and depth of cut are called the cutting conditions. They form the three dimensions of the machining process, and their product can be used to obtain the material removal rate for the process.

title: Roughing and Finishing Cuts
body: Roughing cuts are used to remove a large amount of material rapidly, while finishing cuts complete the part and achieve the final dimension, tolerances, and surface finish. title: Coolant Use in Gun Drilling

title: High Spindle Speeds in Microdrilling
body: Microdrilling requires high spindle speeds exceeding 10,000 RPM and the use of balanced tool holders.

title: Vibration Drilling for Chip Removal
body: Vibration drilling uses axial vibrations to break up chips and remove them from the cutting zone, improving reliability in deep hole drilling.

title: Orbital Drilling for Precision Holes
body: Orbital drilling uses a cutting tool that orbits around the hole center, reducing thrust force and eliminating burrs in metals.

title: Coolant for Chip Flow Management
body: Cutting fluid is used to ease chip flow management, prolong tool life by cooling and lubricating the tip, especially when drilling aluminum.

title: Grinding Cutting Edge for Brass Drilling
body: A face of approximately 1-2 millimeters can be ground on the cutting edge to create an obtuse angle of 91 to 93 degrees, preventing chatter in brass drilling.

title: Peck Drilling for Deep Holes
body: Peck drilling involves plunging the drill part way through the workpiece and retracting it to prevent swarf buildup in deep holes.

title: Use Cutters for Faster Drilling

title: Avoid Burning in Wood Drilling

title: Minimize Chipping in Wood Drilling

title: Optimal RPM Range for Woodworking Lathes

title: Cutting Speeds for Various Materials
body: The cutting speeds are given as constants from material manufacturers or suppliers, available in reference books or charts. These speeds may change based on conditions like coolant use and tool grade.

title: Machinability Rating
body: The machinability rating quantifies how difficult a material is to machine, expressed as a percentage or normalized value. It helps in determining cutting speeds and tool life.

title: Spindle Speed Calculation

title: Constant Surface Speed (CSS)

title: Spindle Speed in Woodworking

title: Speeds for Larger Bits
body: Larger diameter drill bits require slower speeds to avoid burning.

title: Spindle Speeds for Wood vs Metal
body: Drilling wood generally uses higher spindle speeds than metal, but the speed is not as critical.

title: Adjusting Spindle Speeds
body: If cutting conditions are less than ideal, adjustments are made to the spindle's speed, usually a reduction in RPM.

title: Critical Cutting Speed for Stainless Steel
body: Stainless steel requires careful control of cutting speed to avoid overheating and hardening.

title: Chip Thinning Effect
body: When the width of cut is less than half the diameter, chip thinning reduces the actual chipload, requiring increased feed rates.

title: Feed Rate Calculation for Milling
body: The formula FR = RPM × T × CL can be used to determine the feed rate for milling operations.

title: Surface Finish and Feed Rate
body: With a narrow cutter and rapid feed rate, revolution ridges can cause significant variations in surface finish.

title: Trochoidal Marks in Face Milling
body: Face milling produces visible trochoidal marks due to the motion of points on the cutter's end face, affecting surface finish.

title: Improving Surface Finish with Final Pass
body: A final pass with a slow feed rate is used to improve surface finish after removing the bulk of material.

title: Gang Milling for Efficiency
body: Gang milling uses two or more cutters mounted on the same arbor to perform multiple operations simultaneously, improving efficiency.

title: Toolholder Types and Stability

title: HSK Toolholder Advantage
body: HSK toolholders are claimed to be better than BT toolholders at high speeds because their holding mechanism expands with increasing spindle speed, gripping the tool more tightly.

title: Chip Removal in Manual Tapping
body: In manual thread cutting with hand taps, chips are removed by reversing the tap 1/6 of a turn (60 degrees) to break them with the back edges of the cutters. Chips may need to be periodically cleared from the hole, especially for blind holes.

title: Single-Point Threading Process
body: Single-point threading uses a single-point tool to produce threads on a cylinder or cone, with the tool moving linearly while the workpiece rotates to determine thread lead. Typically 5 to 7 light cuts are made to achieve the correct thread depth.

title: CNC Single-Point Threading Advantages
body: CNC lathes allow for quick and easy single-point threading due to spindle synchronization, which tracks the relationship between tool position and spindle position. CNC software includes canned cycles that simplify programming.

title: Thread Milling Chip Evacuation
body: Thread milling offers better chip evacuation compared to cut tapping because it uses a tool the same size as the thread, allowing chips to be removed more efficiently.

title: Thread Milling Advantages
body: Thread milling offers faster cycle times, less tool breakage, and can create left- or right-hand threads with the same tool.

title: Thread Milling vs Tapping
body: Thread milling produces a complete thread profile from the top to the bottom, whereas tapping starts making a complete thread profile on the third thread.

title: Form-Milling Process
body: In form-milling, a single- or multiple-form cutter is used to cut threads in one or two passes by tilting the cutter to the helix angle of the thread and feeding it radially into the blank.

title: Multiple-Form Cutter Limitations
body: Using a multiple-form cutter is faster than using a single-form cutter but is limited to threads with a helix angle less than 3° and blanks of substantial diameter no longer than 2 in (51 mm).

title: Toolpath for Orthogonal Form-Milling
body: In orthogonal form-milling, the cutter's axis is held orthogonally and fed in a toolpath that generates the thread using helical interpolation or small increments of 3-axes linear interpolation.

title: Tooling for Internal Threads
body: Solid cutters are generally limited to holes larger than 6 mm (0.24 in) for internal threads, while indexable tools are limited to holes larger than 12 mm (0.47 in).

title: Thrilling Process
body: Thrilling is a process of threading and drilling internal threads using a specialized cutting tool that drills, chamfers, and threads a hole in one cycle.

title: Helical Broaching Advantages
body: Helical broaching shortens the toolpath of tapping, reducing cycle time and energy consumption.

title: Thread Rolling Material Savings
body: Thread rolling produces no swarf and saves about 15 to 20% in material compared to cutting threads.

title: Thread Rolling Surface Finish
body: Surface finishes from thread rolling range from 6 to 32 micro-inches.

title: Thread Rolling Tolerances
body: Tolerances for thread rolling are typically ±0.001 in (±0.025 mm), with tighter tolerances of ±0.0006 in (±0.015 mm) achievable.

title: Thread Rolling Production Rates
body: Production rates for thread rolling are usually three to five times faster than thread cutting.

title: Thread Forming Tap Lubrication
body: Proper lubrication is essential in thread forming because of frictional forces, so a lubricating oil is used instead of cutting oil.

title: Surface Finish in Boring

title: Limitations of Boring in Geometric Accuracy
body: The limitations of boring in terms of its geometric accuracy (form, position) and the hardness of the workpiece have been shrinking with advances in machining technology. title: Cryogenic Machining Benefits
body: Cryogenic Machining uses cryogenic liquids as coolant to increase tool life and improve surface finish while being environmentally friendly.

title: Pressure or Jet Cooling Method
body: High-pressure water/liquid sprays directly on the machine cutting surface for cooling.

title: Flood Cooling Method
body: Flood cooling uses an oil-water mixture to cover the cutting zone, combining water's cooling ability with oil's lubrication.

title: Cryogenic MQL Machining
body: Combines Cryogenic and MQL methods to reduce cutting area temperature and keep it lubricated.

title: Flooded Cooling System
body: High-pressured, high-volume pumping of oil-water emulsion directly into the tool-chip interface with walls and sump for containment and recirculation.

title: Through-Spindle Coolant Systems
body: Delivers coolant through passages inside the spindle and tool directly to the cutting interface, often at high pressure.

title: Types of Cutting Fluids
body: Includes mineral, semi-synthetic, and synthetic fluids with varying properties for rust inhibition, pH stability, and environmental safety.

title: Water as Cutting Fluid
body: Boils easily, promotes rusting, and does not lubricate well; other ingredients are necessary for optimal performance.

title: Mineral Oils in Cutting Applications
body: Petroleum-based oils used since the late 19th century, varying from thick sulfur-rich to light clear oils.

title: Semi-Synthetic Coolants
body: Emulsion or microemulsion of water with mineral oil, used since the 1930s, known as soluble oil in British English.

title: Synthetic Coolants
body: Water-based, originated in the late 1950s, used for their properties like rust inhibition and environmental safety.

title: Oil Concentration Measurement Techniques
body: Manual titration, refractometer, viscosity measurement, density measurement, and ultrasound speed are used to determine oil concentration in cutting fluids.

title: Alternative Cutting Fluids for Specific Metals
body: Kerosene and rubbing alcohol work well on aluminum, while WD-40 and 3-In-One Oil are suitable for various metals.

title: Way Oil as Cutting Oil
body: Some screw machines use the same oil for both machine ways and cutting, though dedicated way oils are common in commercial machining.

title: Motor Oils as Cutting Fluids
body: Straight-weight non-detergent motor oils can be used, but modern multi-weight motor oils with additives are best avoided due to copper-corrosion concerns.

title: Dielectric Fluid in EDM
body: Used as a cutting fluid in electrical discharge machines, typically deionized water or high-flash-point kerosene.

title: Neatsfoot Oil for Aluminum Machining
body: Used as a cutting fluid for aluminum machining, tapping, and drilling, superior to kerosene and water-based fluids.

title: MQL (Minimum Quantity Lubricant) Delivery
body: MQL delivers aerosol directly through the flutes of the tool, providing precise lubrication at the cutting interface without excessive misting.

title: Carbon Dioxide as a Coolant
body: Pressurized liquid CO2 expands and cools, forming solid crystals that are directed into the cut zone for temperature-controlled cooling.

title: Air as a Coolant
body: Compressed air blows chips away and provides slight cooling through decompression, sometimes with added liquids to form mist.

title: Liquid Nitrogen Cooling
body: Pressurized liquid nitrogen provides cooling through boiling, acting as a 'thermal sponge' to absorb heat from the tool-chip interface.

title: Historical Coolants: Plain Water and Soda Water
body: In the 19th century, plain water was used for cooling cutters, while soda water inhibited rusting of machine slides.

title: Animal Fats as Coolants
body: Animal fats like tallow or lard were popular coolants in the past but are rarely used today due to better alternatives.

title: Safety Concerns with Cutting Fluids
body: Cutting fluids can cause health issues through skin contact and inhalation, including irritation, dermatitis, asthma, and cancer.

title: Maintain Low Fluid Temperature
body: Maintaining as low a fluid temperature as practical will slow the growth of microorganisms.

title: Weekly Testing of Metal Working Fluids
body: Some health and safety regulators require weekly testing of metal working fluids to help maintain the fluid's health, involving checking the bacterial CFU/ml Level and pH level.

title: Use of Skimmers for Tramp Oil Removal
body: Skimmers are used to separate tramp oil from the coolant, involving slowly rotating vertical discs that collect and scrape off the oil.

title: Continuous Separation Effect with CNC Additives
body: CNC additives can manage tramp oil more effectively through a continuous separation effect, allowing easy removal of the accumulated oil.

title: Disposal of Old Cutting Fluid
body: Old, used cutting fluid must be disposed of when it is fetid or chemically degraded and has lost its usefulness.

title: Hand Reamer Lead In
body: A hand reamer has a longer taper or lead in at the front to compensate for the difficulty of starting a hole by hand power alone and to reduce the risk of breakage.

title: Machine Reamer Lead In
body: A machine reamer has a very slight lead in because the reamer and work piece are pre-aligned by the machine, ensuring it starts cutting immediately.

title: Spiral Fluted Reamer Advantage
body: Spiral flutes have the advantage of clearing the swarf automatically.

title: Rose Reamer Relief and Offset
body: A rose reamer has no relief on the periphery and is offset by a front taper to prevent binding.

title: Shell Reamer Design
body: Shell reamers are designed for reaming bearing and other similar items, fluted almost their whole length.

title: Precision Tapered Reamer Usage
body: A precision tapered reamer is used to make a tapered hole for tapered pins, which are self-tightening due to the shallow angle of the taper.

title: Morse Taper Reamer Design
body: A Morse taper reamer is used manually to finish Morse taper sleeves, which are tools for holding machine cutting tools or holders in the spindles of machines.

title: Combination Reamer Material Options
body: Combination reamers can be made out of cobalt, carbide, or high speed steel tooling.

title: Combination Reamer Carbide Tips
body: When using combination reamers to ream large internal diameters made out of material with lower surface feet per minute, carbide tips can be brazed onto a configured drill blank to build the reamer.

title: Combination Reamer Usage Precautions
